 Starting Early Means Coping with El Niño — CCC’s Borje
 Tracy Cabrera November 17, 2026 November 17, 2026 0 8 mins 
 (DC file photo) 
 Climate experts say the Philippines can cope with the looming El Niño crisis by starting early, stressing the that addressing the issue cannot be done by muddling through the problem–recognized as the government’s default mode when faced with a gargantuan task.
According to Climate Change Commission (CCC) vice chairman and executive director Robert E.A. Borje, environment authorities cannot simply “bury their heads in the sand” because many lives and property are at stake if we are not prepared for what some are calling a ‘hellish summer’ in 2027.
 “We must act early on water conservation, protect agriculture, boost local preparedness and use integrated climate forecasts to plan for both drought and sudden floods. A very strong El Niño is already under way, with 41 provinces in rainfall deficit and drought expected to spread nationwide into early 2027. Thus, proactive measures are urgent and needed now,” Secretary Borje pointed out.
 But scientifically, what does the country’s experts know so far about the climate phenomenon and it’s forecasts?
“Very strong El Niño through early 2027 is forecast, with sea surface temperature anomalies peaking at +3.3 degrees Celsius to +3.6 degrees Celsius. Rainfall deficits will intensify, with up to 85 provinces affected by January 2027 and way-below-normal rainfall nationwide by February.
“The crisis will unfold in two phases: floods, which we had seen from July-September 2026 followed by drought (October 2026-May 2027). Heat indices may reach 52 to 55 degrees Celsius, with risks of heat-related deaths,” climatologists explained.
 “We need aggressive water conservation campaigns for households and local government units. Flexible water impounding systems must be in place to store rainfall during intermittent wet periods,” they cited.
Thus, the call of President Ferdinand ‘Bongbong’ Marcos Jr. to buy big drums and begin conserving water is spot-on.
In other countries like Thailand and Indonesia, this is what is being done.
But comparatively to the Philippines, the Thai government has a communications team which is much more savvy in their job. They have asked reputable scientists to help boost support for this water-conserving measure, with the campaign targeted first at far-flung areas.
 In this Borje advised that the government needs to prioritize dam management (e.g., Angat, major Visayas/ Mindanao reservoirs) to stabilize supply for Metro Manila and agricultural zones.
“More solar-powered irrigation systems are required to reduce dependence on hydropower and ensure water access for farms,” he noted.
 “As in other Asian countries, we can adjust our planting calendars to avoid the peak drought months (February to April 2027). We have already urged farmers to shift schedules (but) we also need to promote drought-resistant crop varieties and diversify away from water-intensive crops,” he stressed.
 Environment advocates are proposing now to provide cash assistance and livelihood support, especially for women farmers who face disproportionate impacts. Also needed is the upgrade of post-harvest storage to reduce agricultural losses.
“We have to expect major impacts: agricultural damage already reached P6.87 billion across 14 regions. Hydropower output will drop due to low river flows; some plants (e.g., Bukidnon’s 1.6 MW facility) are already threatened. We must prepare for brownouts as demand rises with extreme heat. We also need to expand solar and wind deployment to reduce reliance on hydropower during drought,” Borje underscored.
 Another proposal is to prepare cooling centers and hydration stations as heat indices climb even as localized efforts include the strengthening of disaster risk reduction offices for dual threats: drought and sudden floods from monsoon bursts.
“In a crisis like this, the most vulnerable groups are the worst affected. We need to monitor them—farmers, fisherfolk, and low-income households—since over 109 million people would be affected,” the CCC’s top executive asserted.
 “We must encourage people to store water early, since rationing of water should be expected in many cities. Electricity use must be reduced during peak hours. Home emergency kits must also be available for both drought and flash floods. We must also support local farmers by buying drought-resilient produce and joining community water-saving initiatives.”
 Finally, Borje advised local government units (LGUs) and the private sector to copy Cebu City’s guidelines for 72 hours of preparedness:
 – Store safe drinking water and build up your food supplies a little at a time.
 – Put together an emergency kit with essentials for 72 hours.
 – Keep important documents in a waterproof pouch and set aside a little cash if you can.
 – Grow vegetables or other food crops if you have space at home.
 “Start with what you already have. Preparing a little at a time can make a difference when your family needs it most. The clock is already ticking,” he eruditely reminded the citizenry.
